meta.title: Who really said "Time spent with cats is never wasted"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Freud never said “Time spent with cats is never wasted.” He disliked cats. The line is an unsourced modern saying, also wrongly credited to Colette.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Time spent with cats is never wasted'?
meta.ogDescription: Freud never said it — he disliked cats. This feel-good line is an unsourced modern saying, credited to Colette in the 1990s and Freud around 2007.

answer.label: Not Sigmund Freud — an unsourced modern saying
answer.authorDates: Falsely pinned on Freud (1856–1939) only around 2007
answer.sourceLine: There is no such line anywhere in Freud’s letters or writings, and quote researchers trace the “cats” wording no earlier than the mid-1990s — when it was first pinned on the French novelist Colette, and only around 2007 on Freud. It most likely began as a folksy American variation of the older saying “Time spent with children is never wasted.” The irony: the one documented remark Freud made about cats is that he did not like them.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Time spent with children is never wasted”

source.excerpt:
“Time spent with cats is never wasted.”

No documented source in Freud’s works supports this. The nearest thing Freud actually wrote about cats came in a letter to his friend Arnold Zweig (10 February 1937): “Ich mag sie nicht. Sie hat die Natur einer Katze, die ich ja auch nicht mag” — “I don’t like her. She has the nature of a cat, which I also don’t like.”
trail: The quote-research site Zitatforschung finds the line in none of Freud’s writings and dates its attribution to him only to around 2007.
The same investigation shows the “cats” wording was first attached to the novelist Colette around 1995 — roughly 40 years after her death — with no source in her French or English works either.
The Freud Museum London lists it among quotes wrongly attributed to Freud, noting he wrote to Arnold Zweig, “I, as is well known, do not like cats.”
A separate collector’s note confirms there is no evidence Freud ever said it, citing the Freud Museum’s own FAQ.
source.excerptNote: The English “cats” aphorism appears to be a modern variation of the older saying “Time spent with children is never wasted,” documented in a 1989 book — not a translation of anything Freud or Colette wrote.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording has no identifiable author or first-publication — it is an anonymous modern saying misattributed to both Freud and Colette — so no copyright status can honestly be asserted. It is not a public-domain line from any documented Freud or Colette work.

author.name: Sigmund Freud
author.heading: About Sigmund Freud
author.bio: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) founded psychoanalysis and reshaped 20th-century ideas about the unconscious, dreams and desire. A famous animal lover in later life, he doted on his chow chow Jofi — but he was decidedly not a cat person: writing to his friend Arnold Zweig, he flatly called cats something he did not like. That makes the cheerful pro-cat aphorism pinned to his name doubly ironic.

misattribution.heading: A feel-good line pinned on the wrong (and unlikely) names
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “magnet name” misquote: a warm, tweetable aphorism grafted onto famous people who never said it — and, in Freud’s case, someone who openly disliked cats.

items.why: The line appears nowhere in Freud’s works or letters; researchers date its attribution to him only to around 2007. Freud actually told Arnold Zweig he did not like cats, and the Freud Museum lists this among quotes he never said.

The novelist Colette (1873–1954) is widely credited with “Time spent with a cat is never wasted,” but the phrase only surfaced under her name around 1995, decades after her death, with no source in her French or English writing.
As with countless feel-good lines, it is sometimes also flung at Einstein — another classic quote-magnet — with no basis whatsoever.

misattribution.truthLine: The likeliest real origin isn’t a great author at all: it reads as a modern spin on the older saying “Time spent with children is never wasted,” recorded in a 1989 book — swap “children” for “cats” and add a famous name.

context.heading: Why this one spreads
lead: Cat lovers want a distinguished ancestor for their affection, and Freud — shorthand for deep insight into the human mind — is an irresistible signature. The joke, unknown to the people sharing it, is that Freud was a dog man who said cats had a “nature” he disliked.
The Colette version is gentler and more plausible — she genuinely wrote about her animals — but plausibility isn’t evidence: no one has found the line in her books, only in 1990s quote collections.
context.pull: Freud didn’t say it — and, unlike most misquotes, he’s on record disagreeing with it.
